synthesis: Targum Jonathan renders Joel 1:1 with characteristic expansions that clarify the prophetic nature of the communication and distance the divine word from direct human contact. The substitution of פִּתְגַם נְבוּאָה ('word of prophecy') for the MT's דְּבַר יְהוָה ('word of the LORD') and the addition of מִן קֳדָם ('from before') exemplify standard Targumic strategies of theological mediation and explicitation of prophetic genre. The rendering otherwise follows the MT closely in structure and personnel, with only minor lexical shifts.

word_analysis.note: The MT's simple 'word' is expanded into 'word of prophecy,' making explicit the prophetic genre that is implicit in the superscription.
The divine name is preceded by מִן קֳדָם ('from before'), a standard Targumic distancing formula that avoids the implication of direct divine speech to a human.
The relative pronoun is rendered idiomatically in Aramaic as a relative clause particle with the verb 'was/came,' closely following the MT syntax.
The Hebrew qal perfect of היה is rendered by the Aramaic cognate הוה, a near-literal lexical equivalent.
The MT preposition אֶל ('to/unto') is replaced by עִם ('with'), softening the directness of divine speech directed at the prophet.
The proper name is transliterated directly with standard Aramaic orthography, showing no deviation.
The Hebrew 'son of' is replaced by its standard Aramaic equivalent בַּר, a routine lexical substitution.
The patronym is transliterated directly without alteration, preserving the MT reading against some traditions.

theological_modifications.targ_reading: פִּתְגַם נְבוּאָה מִן קֳדָם יְיָ דַהֲוָה עִם
theological_modifications.explanation: The combination of מִן קֳדָם ('from before') and עִם ('with') instead of אֶל ('to') softens the anthropomorphic intimacy of direct divine speech to a human prophet. This dual modification reflects the Targumic concern, analyzed by Grossfeld and Smelik, to maintain transcendence by interposing distance formulae between God and human recipients of revelation. The 'from before' formula is pervasive in Targum Jonathan to the Prophets and functions as a quasi-technical marker of mediated divine communication.

targumic_expansions.midrashic_parallel: The phrase פִּתְגַם נְבוּאָה is a standard Targumic prophetic superscription formula appearing in Targum Jonathan to Hosea 1:1, Amos 1:1, Micah 1:1, and others, suggesting a formulaic editorial layer in the Targum of the Twelve.
targumic_expansions.significance: The expansion explicates the prophetic genre of the book, functioning as a hermeneutical label that categorizes what follows as prophetic discourse rather than general divine communication; this reflects the Targumic tendency noted by McNamara to clarify the mode of revelation.

The distancing formula מִן קֳדָם is an addition not present in either the MT or LXX and represents the standard Targumic theological buffer between the divine and human spheres, consistent with the broader tendencies of Targum Jonathan described by Smelik (1995).

lxx_alignment.areas_of_agreement: Both the LXX (λόγος κυρίου) and the Targum render דְּבַר יְהוָה with a single nominal equivalent for 'word' (λόγος / פִּתְגַם), and both preserve 'Petuel/Bathouel' as the patronym rather than offering an alternative reading. The LXX uses πρός ('to/toward') like the MT's אֶל, while the Targum substitutes עִם, so they diverge at this point.
lxx_alignment.significance: The shared preservation of the Petuel patronym against variant traditions suggests both translators worked from a proto-MT textual tradition; the divergence in the prepositional rendering of divine address shows independent theological interpretation rather than a shared Vorlage variant.

key_divergences.explanation: The single Hebrew noun 'word' becomes a construct phrase 'word of prophecy' in the Targum, a formulaic expansion that is the most significant structural addition and is characteristic of Targum Jonathan's superscriptions to the Twelve Prophets.

The replacement of אֶל ('to') with עִם ('with') subtly alters the directional force of divine speech, suggesting accompaniment or presence rather than direct address, which aligns with broader Targumic tendencies to reduce anthropomorphic directness in divine-human communication.

The addition of מִן קֳדָם before the divine name is the most theologically significant intervention in the verse, establishing a spatial and hierarchical buffer between God and the prophet that is absent in both the MT and LXX.

assessment.title: Formulaic Prophetic Superscription with Characteristic Theological Distancing in Targum Jonathan
assessment.reasoning: Targum Jonathan's rendering of Joel 1:1 exemplifies the standard editorial and theological strategy applied consistently across the Targum of the Twelve Prophets: a formulaic superscription (פִּתְגַם נְבוּאָה) categorizes the book as prophetic, while מִן קֳדָם and the substitution of עִם for אֶל together construct a mediated theological distance between God and prophet. These moves reflect what Smelik identifies as the Targum's systematic reduction of anthropomorphic immediacy in prophetic discourse, and what Grossfeld describes as the interposition of mediatorial language. The otherwise close rendering of proper names and syntactic structure demonstrates that the Targum translator was working faithfully from a text substantially identical to the MT, with expansions and substitutions driven by theological convention rather than textual uncertainty. The absence of any messianic or eschatological reinterpretation in this superscription verse is consistent with the Targum's treatment of prophetic titles as primarily genre-labeling rather than typological sites.
assessment.plain: The Aramaic translation of Joel 1:1 stays very close to the Hebrew original but makes two key changes: it labels the book explicitly as 'a word of prophecy' to make the genre clear, and it adds the phrase 'from before the LORD' to avoid saying that God spoke directly to the prophet, softening the intimacy of divine-human communication. These are standard features of the Aramaic translation tradition for the Prophets.
assessment.next_steps: A systematic comparison of the superscription formula פִּתְגַם נְבוּאָה across all twelve Minor Prophets in Targum Jonathan would clarify whether the formula is editorially uniform or shows variation; additionally, examination of the substitution of עִם for אֶל across Targum Jonathan's prophetic corpus would illuminate whether this reflects a consistent theological principle or is verse-specific.
